# Mr. Patel's Careful Steps

Mr. Patel sits in the therapy office with his hands folded in his lap, his weathered fingers still bearing the calluses of forty-eight years spent as an electrician. At seventy-six, he has largely retired, though he occasionally helps his son with residential wiring jobs—work that once brought him genuine satisfaction. Now, even stepping outside his house requires a calculation that exhausts him before the day begins.

The mugging happened eight months ago on an ordinary Tuesday evening. Mr. Patel had walked to the corner market near his home in the same neighborhood where he and his wife have lived for thirty-two years. The route was familiar, the walk manageable for his aging knees. He was thinking about what vegetables his wife had asked him to buy when two young men approached from behind. They grabbed his wallet, his phone, and pushed him hard against the brick wall of a closed storefront. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds, but Mr. Patel remembers it in fragments—the smell of their cologne, the specific angle of the pavement as his face scraped against it, the sound of his own breathing, rapid and panicked.

Since that evening, Mr. Patel's world has contracted considerably. He no longer walks to the market. His wife now handles the shopping, though she is seventy-four and has her own health concerns. When Mr. Patel does leave the house—for medical appointments, for his grandson's birthday party—he experiences a mounting dread that begins hours beforehand. His chest tightens. His palms sweat. He finds himself scanning every face on the street, every shadow between parked cars. At the market with his wife, he positions himself with his back to the wall, unable to relax even in broad daylight.

The nights are often worse. Mr. Patel lies awake beside his wife, his mind replaying the assault in vivid detail. Sometimes he jolts awake, his heart racing, convinced that someone is in their bedroom. He has begun sleeping in the living room several nights a week, telling his wife it is because of his back pain, though they both know the truth. The intrusive images come without warning during the day as well—while he is reading the newspaper, while he is watching television, while he sits in his son's truck on the way to help with a wiring job.

His son noticed the change first. Mr. Patel had always been the steady one, the man who could climb a ladder without hesitation, who never complained about difficult jobs. Now his son finds him reluctant to leave the house, anxious about the simplest outings. When his son asked directly about the mugging, Mr. Patel became irritable, insisting it was nothing, that he was fine, that he simply preferred to stay home. But his wife sees the way he checks the locks multiple times before bed, the way he flinches at unexpected sounds, the way he has withdrawn from the family gatherings he once enjoyed.

Mr. Patel describes himself as a practical man, someone who has always solved problems through hard work and determination. The idea that he cannot simply "move past" the mugging troubles him deeply. He feels ashamed of his fear, embarrassed that he cannot walk to the market alone. There is a heaviness to his days now, a sense that he is not fully living but rather existing within an increasingly smaller space, waiting for safety that never quite arrives.
